q: After shift report, which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client 2 days after hip surgery reporting pain of 5/10 who is due for oral analgesia
A client with COPD whose SpO2 is 90% on 2 L/min nasal cannula
A client 1 hour after thyroidectomy with a hoarse voice and new noisy, high-pitched breathing
A client with type 2 diabetes whose pre-breakfast glucose is 180 mg/dL (10 mmol/L)
why: New stridor after thyroidectomy suggests airway compromise from edema, hematoma or laryngeal nerve injury — an airway problem comes first (ABCs). An SpO2 around 90% can be an expected target for many clients with COPD, and the other findings are stable.

q: Which task is most appropriate for the RN to delegate to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?
options: Teaching a newly diagnosed client how to self-inject insulin
Measuring vital signs for a stable client on post-operative day 2
Assessing pain 30 minutes after IV morphine
Evaluating a client’s understanding of a low-sodium diet
why: UAP may perform routine tasks such as vital signs for stable clients. Assessment, teaching and evaluation require the nursing judgment of the RN and cannot be delegated.

q: Which client assignment is most appropriate for a licensed practical/registered practical nurse (LPN/RPN)?
options: Completing the admission assessment for a client with new chest pain
Giving scheduled oral medications to a client with stable chronic heart failure
Creating the plan of care for a client admitted from the ICU
Providing first-time discharge teaching for a new colostomy
why: Practical nurses care for stable clients with predictable outcomes, including scheduled oral medications. Initial assessments, care planning for unstable or new clients and initial teaching fall within the RN role in most jurisdictions.

q: A client about to sign a surgical consent says, “I’m not really sure what the surgeon is going to remove.” What should the nurse do?
options: Explain the procedure in detail and have the client sign
Witness the signature because the client is alert and oriented
Hold the consent and notify the surgeon to explain the procedure
Ask a family member to sign on the client’s behalf
why: Informed consent is the prescriber’s responsibility. The nurse witnesses the signature and confirms understanding; if the client is unsure, the nurse stops and notifies the surgeon before the consent is signed.

q: Which action by a nurse is a breach of client confidentiality?
options: Discussing a client’s new diagnosis with a coworker in a hospital elevator
Sharing relevant findings during bedside handover with the oncoming nurse
Logging out of the electronic record before leaving the workstation
Giving information to the client’s designated substitute decision-maker
why: Discussing identifiable health information in public spaces violates privacy law and professional standards. Handover to the care team and sharing with an authorised decision-maker are appropriate.

q: After caring for a client with Clostridioides difficile diarrhea, which hand hygiene method is most appropriate?
options: Removing gloves without further hand hygiene
why: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol does not reliably destroy. Soap and water mechanically remove spores. Contact precautions with gown and gloves are also used.

q: A client is admitted with suspected active pulmonary tuberculosis. Which precautions are required?
options: A surgical mask for staff and the door left open
A fit-tested N95 (or higher) respirator and an airborne infection isolation room
Droplet precautions in a semi-private room
why: TB spreads by airborne droplet nuclei. Airborne precautions require a negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room and a fit-tested respirator for staff.

q: Which transmission-based precautions are used for a hospitalised client with influenza?
why: Influenza is spread mainly by large respiratory droplets. Droplet precautions — a mask when within close range and a private room or cohorting — are used in addition to standard precautions.

q: Which action by a new nurse caring for a client with soft wrist restraints requires the charge nurse to intervene?
options: Securing the restraint to the movable side rail
Checking skin, circulation and need at intervals set by policy
Ensuring two fingers fit under the restraint
why: Restraints are tied to the bed frame, not the side rail — lowering the rail can injure the client. The other actions are correct practice.

q: Which intervention is most appropriate for an older adult at high risk for falls?
options: Raise all four side rails at night
Keep the bed in the lowest position with wheels locked and the call light in reach
Apply a vest restraint while the client sleeps
Turn all lights off at night to promote sleep
why: A low, locked bed with the call light in reach reduces injury risk. Four raised rails and restraints can increase injury when clients climb over; a night light improves visibility.

q: Before giving digoxin to an adult, the nurse finds an apical pulse of 54 beats/min. What is the best action?
options: Give the dose and recheck the pulse in 1 hour
Hold the dose and notify the prescriber per protocol
Recheck using the radial pulse and give if it is above 50
why: Digoxin slows heart rate; it is commonly held when the adult apical pulse is below 60 beats/min. The nurse should also review potassium and digoxin levels and follow the prescriber’s parameters.

q: A prescription reads “potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push.” What should the nurse do?
options: Clarify the order — IV potassium is never given by push
Dilute it in 10 mL of saline and push
why: IV push potassium can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias. IV potassium must be diluted and infused at a controlled rate using a pump, per policy.

q: A client taking warfarin has an INR of 6.2 and bleeding gums. Which medication should the nurse anticipate?
why: Vitamin K reverses warfarin’s effect. Protamine reverses heparin, naloxone reverses opioids and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.

q: A client on a continuous heparin infusion develops significant bleeding. Which reversal agent should the nurse anticipate?
why: Protamine sulfate neutralises unfractionated heparin. The infusion is stopped and the prescriber notified.

q: A client taking lithium has a serum level of 1.9 mEq/L. Which findings should the nurse expect?
options: Vomiting, diarrhea and a coarse hand tremor
Peaked T waves on the ECG
why: The usual maintenance range is roughly 0.6–1.2 mEq/L. Levels above that cause GI upset, coarse tremor, weakness and confusion. Teach consistent fluid and sodium intake.

q: Which insulin can be given by IV infusion?
why: Regular (short-acting) insulin is the insulin used for IV infusions, such as in diabetic ketoacidosis. Long-acting and intermediate-acting insulins are given subcutaneously only.

q: A client with preeclampsia is receiving IV magnesium sulfate. Which finding requires the nurse to stop the infusion?
options: Respiratory rate 10/min and absent patellar reflexes
why: Loss of deep tendon reflexes and respiratory depression are signs of magnesium toxicity. Stop the infusion, notify the provider and have calcium gluconate available.

q: Which ECG change is most associated with hyperkalemia?
options: A shortened QT interval from hypercalcemia
why: Hyperkalemia classically causes tall, peaked T waves and can progress to a widened QRS and dangerous arrhythmias. U waves suggest hypokalemia.

q: Which finding should the nurse expect in a client with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?
why: DKA causes hyperglycemia and metabolic acidosis; the body compensates with deep, rapid Kussmaul breathing to blow off CO2. Fruity breath and dehydration are also common.

q: A client with chest trauma suddenly becomes hypotensive and dyspneic. Which finding suggests tension pneumothorax?
options: Trachea deviated away from the injured side
Slow respirations with normal blood pressure
why: Rising pressure in the affected pleural space pushes the mediastinum and trachea toward the unaffected side, compromising venous return. It is an emergency requiring immediate decompression.

q: The nurse notes continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber of a chest drainage system. What does this indicate?
options: An air leak in the system or from the client
why: Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber suggests an air leak. The nurse checks connections from the client to the unit and follows policy. Tidaling (rise and fall with breathing) is expected.

q: A client arrives with sudden facial droop and arm weakness. Which information is most important in deciding eligibility for thrombolytic therapy?
options: The time the client was last known to be well
why: Thrombolytics for ischemic stroke are time-dependent — commonly within 3 hours and up to 4.5 hours of onset for selected clients — so last-known-well time is critical.

q: Which is an early sign of hypovolemic shock?
why: Compensatory sympathetic activation causes tachycardia, anxiety or restlessness and cool skin early, before blood pressure falls.

q: Which statement by a client with heart failure shows understanding of daily weights?
options: “I’ll weigh myself every morning after I urinate and before breakfast, and call if I gain 2–3 lb (about 1 kg) in a day.”
“I’ll weigh myself once a week after dinner.”
“Weight changes don’t matter as long as my ankles aren’t swollen.”
“I’ll only weigh myself when I feel short of breath.”
why: Daily weights at the same time, on the same scale and in similar clothing detect fluid retention early. Rapid gain (often 2–3 lb/1–1.5 kg in a day or 5 lb/2.3 kg in a week) should be reported.

q: A client in a new forearm cast reports severe pain unrelieved by opioids. Which additional finding is most concerning?
options: Pain that increases when the nurse passively extends the fingers
Mild swelling of the fingers that improves with elevation
Warm, pink fingers with brisk capillary refill
why: Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch are early signs of compartment syndrome, a surgical emergency. Notify the provider immediately and keep the limb at heart level.

q: What is the most reliable method to confirm initial placement of a blind-inserted nasogastric feeding tube?
options: Auscultating an air bolus over the stomach
Checking that the client can speak
Measuring the external tube length only
why: X-ray is the gold standard for confirming initial placement before feeding or medication. Air-bolus auscultation is unreliable. pH testing and marked length help with ongoing checks.

q: Fifteen minutes into a blood transfusion, the client reports chills and low back pain and has a temperature of 38.6 °C. What is the first action?
why: These signs suggest an acute transfusion reaction. Stop the transfusion first, keep the IV open with normal saline using new tubing, stay with the client and notify the provider and blood bank.

q: Which post-operative finding should the nurse report to the surgeon?
options: Urine output of 20 mL/hr for the past 2 hours
Serous drainage on the dressing edge
why: Adult urine output below about 30 mL/hr (or 0.5 mL/kg/hr) may signal hypovolemia or renal hypoperfusion and should be reported.

q: The day after a total thyroidectomy, which finding requires immediate follow-up?
options: Tingling around the mouth and muscle twitching
A small amount of serous drainage
why: Perioral tingling and twitching (positive Chvostek or Trousseau sign) indicate hypocalcemia from parathyroid injury. Notify the provider; IV calcium gluconate may be needed.

q: Which description matches a stage 2 pressure injury?
options: Partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis or an intact or ruptured serum-filled blister
Full-thickness tissue loss with visible fat
Full-thickness loss with exposed bone or tendon
why: Stage 1 is non-blanchable erythema of intact skin; stage 2 is partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis; stages 3 and 4 involve full-thickness loss.

q: To reduce aspiration risk for a client receiving continuous enteral feeding, the nurse should:
options: Keep the head of the bed elevated at least 30–45 degrees
Place the client flat for comfort
Check residuals only once a day
Hang a 24-hour supply of formula at once
why: Head-of-bed elevation of at least 30–45 degrees during feeding reduces aspiration. Formula hang times follow policy to limit contamination.

q: After giving IV morphine, when should the nurse reassess the client’s pain and sedation?
why: IV opioids act quickly; reassess pain, sedation and respiratory status within about 15–30 minutes (oral routes typically 30–60 minutes), per policy.

q: Which milestone should the nurse expect in a healthy 6-month-old?
options: Sits with support and transfers objects hand to hand
Builds a tower of four blocks
why: Around 6 months infants roll over, sit with support and begin transferring objects. Walking alone typically emerges near 12 months; word combinations and block towers come later.

q: Which vaccine is contraindicated during pregnancy?
why: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine and is not given during pregnancy. Tdap and inactivated influenza are recommended in pregnancy.

q: A postpartum client has heavy bleeding and a soft, boggy uterus. What is the nurse’s first action?
options: Notify the provider before doing anything
Place the client in high Fowler’s position
why: Uterine atony is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Fundal massage promotes contraction first; then empty the bladder, give uterotonics as ordered and escalate.

q: Late decelerations appear on the fetal monitor while oxytocin is infusing. Which action is the priority?
why: Late decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency. Stop oxytocin, reposition to the side, give IV fluids, apply oxygen per protocol and notify the provider.

q: A child presents with high fever, drooling and a tripod position. Which action should the nurse avoid?
options: Examining the throat with a tongue depressor
Keeping the child calm on the parent’s lap
why: These findings suggest epiglottitis. Inspecting the throat can trigger complete airway obstruction; keep the child calm and prepare for advanced airway support.

q: A client says, “It won’t matter much longer anyway.” What is the nurse’s best response?
options: “Don’t talk like that — you have so much to live for.”
why: Asking directly and clearly about suicidal thoughts is the recommended approach and does not increase risk. Reassurance, changing the subject and generalising block communication.

q: A client whose last drink was 8 hours ago now has tremors, anxiety, sweating and a heart rate of 112. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Early alcohol withdrawal requiring monitoring with a validated scale
why: Alcohol withdrawal often begins within 6–24 hours of the last drink. Use a scale such as CIWA-Ar, give benzodiazepines per protocol and monitor for seizures and delirium.

q: After being criticised by his manager, a client comes home and shouts at his dog. Which defense mechanism is he using?
why: Displacement redirects feelings from the real source to a safer target. Projection attributes one’s own feelings to others; sublimation channels them into acceptable activity.

q: Amoxicillin 500 mg is prescribed. The suspension available is 250 mg per 5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
why: Desired ÷ have × quantity = 500 ÷ 250 × 5 mL = 10 mL.

q: 1,000 mL of normal saline is to infuse over 8 hours using tubing with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. What is the rate in drops per minute?
why: 1,000 mL × 15 gtt/mL ÷ 480 min = 31.25, rounded to 31 gtt/min. (The pump rate would be 125 mL/hr.)

q: Heparin 25,000 units in 500 mL D5W is to run at 1,000 units/hour. What rate should the nurse set on the pump?
why: Concentration = 25,000 ÷ 500 = 50 units/mL. 1,000 units/hr ÷ 50 units/mL = 20 mL/hr. Heparin is high-alert — use an independent double check.

q: A child weighs 22 lb. The prescribed dose is 15 mg/kg/dose. How many mg is one dose?
why: 22 lb ÷ 2.2 = 10 kg; 10 kg × 15 mg/kg = 150 mg. Always confirm the dose is within the safe range for the drug.
